title: The uncle leaves 70% of its £ 500k assets to charity, so who pays the inheritance tax bill?
text:
My wife is an executor of her uncle’s will. It has a assets valued at approximately 500,000.
It leaves 70 percent to several charities and the remaining 30 percent to the family.
First, my wife was told that he could be responsible for any tax that beneficial organizations have to pay, what do I think it is incorrect?
Second, if the value of the heritage remains at £ 500,000 and grants 70 percent (£ 350,000) to the beneficial organization, the remaining £ 150,000, because it is below the threshold of £ 325,000, will be responsible for any tax of any tax of inheritance? Would you please help?
Tanya Jefferies, this is money, replies: This is a good question because leaving some charity in your will is something wonderful, but it can affect how your heritage is managed and there are some difficulties to avoid.
The problems that people should consider are covered in a recent guide of this is money: Leaving money to charity in your will: how to create a legacy and reduce your IHT bill.
Regarding his question, we asked a financial expert with many years of experience in helping people plan inheritance and solve properties to answer below.
Ian Dyall: Executors can be personally responsible if the administration of heritage is wrong
Ian Dyall, head of patrimonial planning at Evelyn Partners, replies: Let me start with the good news and then I will provide a little history that can explain where I think the confusion may have come.
First, provided that his wife manages heritage as best and is not negligent, it should not be personally responsible before any tax on assets and can claim the cost of administering the assets of assets of the heritage.
You don’t say if your uncle is alive or has died.
However, according to the current value of the heritage and the amount that goes to charity, there should be no inheritance imposed unless there are (or significant gifts of your uncle in the last seven years of your life that use part of the part of the £ 325,000 null rate band.
So why could someone tell his wife that he could be responsible for any tax that beneficial organizations have to pay?
Executors can be personally responsible if they are wrong in the administration of heritage. For example, a few years ago, an executor administered the heritage of £ 1.2 million of a friend that largely consisted of properties.
He paid enough inheritance tax to obtain a subsidy of successions that leave £ 340,000 not paid (which is possible with the property, if he pays the invoice for interests with interest).
Then, the executor distributed the rest to the beneficiary, in the understanding that the beneficiary would pay the remaining inheritance tax as it expired.
The beneficiary quickly moved to Barbados leaving the unstable bill. The courts considered that the executor is personally responsible for the debt.
The moral is that, if you are an executor, do not be too hurried to pay the income to the beneficiaries.
Make sure you have definitely identified all possible beneficiaries and maintain enough funds to pay all debts that assets, including the tax.
BENEFICAL ORGANIZATIONS are exempt from paying the inheritance tax
How does the gift fits for charity in this? I am not completely clear about what his wife has told him, who told him, and how much they know about the value of his uncle’s heritage. However, the following can be the root of confusion.
When money in a heritage leaves in part to a person or organization exempt from the inheritance tax, as a beneficial organization, and the rest goes to the people who are not exempt (for example, children, nephews, nieces), then the Question is, how is the load of the shared inheritance tax?
List the tax over the whole assets and then divide the rest 70:30? In which case, the beneficial organization is effectively receiving a reduced amount due to the inheritance tax, although it is exempt from paying the inheritance tax.
Or the charity should obtain 70 percent of the gross assets before taxes, with nothing deduced, since it is exempt from the inheritance tax, and the rest of the assets pay the entire inheritance tax?
A good lawyer will be aware of this problem and will be clear in the will on which of the above options must be applied.
However, the predetermined option is usually the second in which the beneficial organization does not suffer any of the taxes. This actually leads to a lower tax on general inheritance, but less to beneficiaries who are not charity.
You can see that it can (lazy) describe the second option as executors who are responsible before any inheritance tax on the participation of the beneficial organization. This may have been what meant when they told his wife that he would be “responsible for any tax that beneficial organizations have to pay.”
Fortunately, where appropriate the question seems to be academic.
Whenever there is no (or no) significant gifts for the wife’s uncle in the seven years prior to his death, the farm should have an £ 325,000 rate (or more if he has a null rate band transferable a deceased spouse).
The gift for the beneficial organization is exempt and the residue must fall into the void rate.
